correctness.rationale: The sharp sandwich is converted exactly to b_infinity^2 h_Z^2 <= q <= h_Z^2 for the quadratic support form q. Group averaging preserves these inequalities. The source proof of Theorem 5.3 strictly excludes every invariant shape alpha != 1. Horizontal and minimizing-slope contacts fix the averaged scale, and equality of a continuous nonnegative integrand with zero Haar average forces equality on each relevant orbit. Those orbit equalities determine every block of the original quadratic form, giving Q=b_infinity^2 I. The proof is analytic for every n>=3; no finite computation is promoted to an infinite conclusion.

evidence: F. Grundbacher and T. Kobos, arXiv:2407.08829v2, Corollary 2.11: uniqueness is guaranteed for symmetric K only under d_BM(K,B_2^n)>sqrt(n-1).
For the Gaussian zonoid, phi(s)>=1 and phi(s)>=s imply F_1(s)>=1/sqrt(2), hence d_BM(Z_n,B_2^n)=b_infinity^{-1}<=sqrt(2); therefore the Corollary 2.11 hypothesis fails for every n>=3.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The most relevant broader theorem does not dominate the claim in the stated dimensions. General higher-dimensional distance ellipsoids can be nonunique, so uniqueness cannot be inferred from a universal theorem without additional hypotheses.

value.rationale: Distance ellipsoids can be nonunique in dimensions at least three, so optimizer uniqueness is a structural issue. The recent Gaussian-zonoid theorem determines the exact Banach--Mazur constant but leaves open whether nonsymmetric sharp ellipsoids survive the averaging step. The contact-orbit equality argument resolves precisely that natural gap for the whole new family, giving a reusable rigidity mechanism without relying on a routine numerical check or a cosmetic reformulation.
